newsitem.title: LATVIA: FOCUS-New Latvian finance minister voted in.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-New Latvian finance minister voted in.

text.p: New Latvian Finance Minister Robert Zile was voted into office on Thursday, filling a post that had been vacant since October and had stirred a controversy which brought down the previous government.
Zile, up to now the head of the parliament budget and finance committee, is a member of the third-largest party in Latvia's eight-party coalition government.
His main task in 1997 will be to make sure that the government meets its target of a balanced budget, a key plank of the economic policy of Prime Minister Andris Shkele.

The finance post has been one of the most sensitive for Shkele to fill since he originally came to power at the end of 1995 with a promise of fiscal austerity and a pledge to drag Latvia out of the mess caused by a serious banking crisis.
Zile told Latvian radio that there was no need to worry about balancing the 1997 budget and said he favoured more deficit-free budgets in future.
"I would like to see a normal balanced budget also for next year and some conceptual matters to be clarified already for 1999," Zile said on radio after the vote.
The previous finance minister resigned in October 1996 and a row between Shkele and President Guntis Ulmanis in January over a new minister caused the fall of Shkele's former government.

Shkele quit in fury after Ulmanis called on parliament to reject the candidature of businessman Vassily Melnik to the finance post after reports that Melnik had been investigated by the prosecutor's office.
Shkele and Ulmanis later settled their differences and Shkele was recalled to the premier's post.
His new government took office two weeks ago after Melnik had resigned days after being voted into office.
Zile has also said he backs more order in the tax system to make it more predictable for businessmen and the public.
He says he wants new taxes to be introduced only in the following calendar year or if the budget is amended by parliament.
Sudden changes in law are one of the main complaints of foreign investors when doing business in Latvia.
Zile also said he backed a transparent system, so that people could see clearly where money was being spent.
"Any spare funds that the budget receives should be spent on social services and on the improvement of the state revenue service. This is what earns money," he added.
Financial sources have generally given a warm reception to Zile's appointment.
"Zile is a very good choice from the point of view of financial institutions," said Ivar Kirsons, vice-president of leading bank, Unibanka.
"For me, Zile was the best choice in the circumstances," he added.
